title: GIMP now has UI tests (gimp.org)
comments: Having only 13 tests to start is actually a healthy sign for a GUI codebase this old. The hard part of desktop UI testing is almost never writing the 14th through 200th test -- it's building a deterministic harness that doesn't flake on window-manager focus races, font/DPI differences, or async redraw timing.Once you have a small suite that reliably catches real regressions without false positives in CI, adding one regression test per fixed UI bug scales much better than trying to assert on every widget up front. Huge generated UI suites usually end up cementing accidental layout behavior and training contributors to ignore red builds.reply

title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8) (github.com/openssl)
comments: On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB.  EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it.  But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.You should probably assume that, if you are running anything that can be convinced to use this API to encode a very long blob as base64, then you are in trouble. I don’t know why a modern server would do this.BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs.  Stay away.edit: Fixed my size threshold, hopefully. I was thinking of unsigned ints, but this is a signed int. I have not looked at the code, just the description.reply

> BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.We’ve known this for well over two decade since heartbleed yet for some reason Linux distros haven’t migrated off of itreply
For those too young to remember 2014, Heartbleed led to both BoringSSL and LibreSSL being forked from OpenSSL.reply
TIL it's 2036reply

To be fair, frustrations with OpenSSL long preceded Heartbleed. Heartbleed was just the final straw for those who forked libressl and BoringSSL.And to be fair to OpenSSL, it was one of the first widely used crypto libraries, along with Netscape's NSS. Setting aside the reasonablebess of the initial choices, the rapid uptake meant those choices were difficult if not impossible to completely unwind, particularly the style and typing of parameters and error reporting. Even today debates rage about signed vs unsigned, etc, in C and other languages. (But suffice it to say there are still alot of unforced errors, IMO, such as implicit output buffer sizes.)reply
Not breaking userspace is more important than security………reply

The bottom line is that this doesn't appear to be easily exploitable and IMHO it should be the callers of EVP_EncodeBlock which need to be inspected to determine the actual risk.using a nontrivial formulaIt's base64. 4/3 expansion; round it up and add padding. What's "nontrivial" about that?and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate itNot necessary, because the caller is responsible for allocation.reply

first_paragraph: This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" (CVE-2026-121481) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock(): NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int. The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending.Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock().I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock(). No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int, but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths.Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c, which rejected only len > INT_MAX.I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod.Exploiting this vulnerability from the command l

title: Postgres 19 Repack: Faster, Built-In Table Bloat Cleanup (snowflake.com)
comments: I haven't used these extensions, but I like the direction of being able to extend Postgres by tailing its own internals (pg_squeeze approach) than triggers (pg_repack).We (the SpiceDB developers) took a similar approach to solve a different problem a few years ago: implementing strict serializability in Postgres[0]. By hooking into the transactions layer themselves (pg_xact), we could layer on our own MVCC reusing the real Postgres transactions to compute visibility and total ordering. When you can just tail the Postgres internals, you don't even need to implement a Postgres extension, which can keep it portable across locked-down, managed Postgres offerings.Do folks know of other clever implementations of behavior by "spying" on the Postgres internals?[0]: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_f6fHy4DWWMreply

Physicist here. I don't have time right now to read the papers in depth, nor are the results directly in my area, but I would say a few things.One is that there are a near-infinite number of "open problems" in physics because the surface area of research programs in theoretical physics is extremely large. Before I was in the world of physics, I would have thought that "solving an open problem" meant that physicists around the world would be rejoicing and discussing the result. In reality, other than for the big, field-defining questions, only a small handful of people might care about any problem being solved. That holds true even for the Millennium problems.Even if I were to read these papers in depth and understand them, without talking to somebody that knows the area and what has been done in it already, I would have no sense of the significance. The way to assess significance is to see how the community responds. Only time will tell whether people care about these results enough to cite them, incorporate them in future work, etc.And so, like many other people I know, I plan to ignore all of these results until somebody I know comes and tells me to check one out: the cost of assessing any of them is too high, and there are too many other papers to read.reply

In physics if you have a important open problem, you can probably just throw numerics at it to compare theory with experiment. title: The 98% Slot Machine: How Paid Advertising Became an Extraction Tax (globalcommercegraph.com)
comments: This analogy doesn't hold at all. Casinos are engineered for the house to win and the customer to lose because the casino is paying the customer directly. They are disincentivized to let the customer win. If the customer always won, the casino goes out of business very quickly.Ad auctions are completely different, since they are just a marketplace. A customer's (advertiser's) win comes from a third party, and the point of the ad platform is to connect that third party to the customer. The ad platform would love to be able to make every single customer win all the time. Although, if they did that, it would create a lot more demand and even out the ROI with increased ad prices. But that's not the "evil ad platform" engineering the customers to always lose in the way casinos do, that's simply basic supply/demand economics.COI disclaimer: My current job is a small part of an ads platform on a website you have heard of. I dislike ads but realize they are a necessity for running some parts of the internet.reply

Yea, I also work in ads and the article doesn't make sense at all. A way bigger factor than anything mentioned in this article is simply what you as an advertiser can afford as a CAC (cost to acquire a customer). There are some advertisers who are selling low cost/low repeat products that advertising is nearly impossible to make profitable. Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.Many companies are spending significant amounts of money (many millions) and not even telling the advertising platforms the actual revenue they generated from the ads, just the number of "leads" or "customers" because they are paranoid about the very thing in the article (which I don't actually believe to be true anyway).reply

> Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.This is correct. Those advertisers were willing to buy pretty much the whole inventory at a price a startup focusing on say a single niche SO tag couldn't compete with.Disclosure: Work on an ad startup I helped build. I talk to over a dozen advertisers every day. We have similar problems with advertisers trying to buy most/all of our inventory and we explicitly cap the max percentage we'll sell to any one advertiser.reply

For the rest of us it just reminds us that the next time we buy a car we're going to drive 50 miles to a town where one guy doesn't own all the new car dealerships.If a radio ad costs him $20 I am sure he gets at least $20 of pleasure from hearing his name and he makes monopoly profits so he can afford it!A similar story was that a tiny ad in the local newspaper cost $100 a day and it was stupendously difficult to make a case that this was worth it for most small businesses,  especially when you could get a storefront for that much or hire a part-timer. We did know it was a potential security risk, and that is why it was handled exactly how security-sensitive issues are supposed to be handled (not to mention that the reporter is a well-respected OpenJDK contributor and former Oracle colleague).I don't know if people here understand how these things need to be done in the most important and critical open source projects, such as Linux or OpenJDK, but there are two things you must not do when an issue is suspected to be a risk until you've researched the matter and decided on a backport and release strategy: You shouldn't communicate publicly, and you absolutely shouldn't merge a patch.reply

> You shouldn't communicate publicly, and you absolutely shouldn't merge a patch.I (still) agree, but I don't think these rules will be valid for much longer, though.With new models capable of finding vulnerabilities faster than ever before, if you (or your AI) was able to find a critical bug, it's only a matter of time that the bad guys will also discover it - if they haven't already.Human skill and ingenuity used to be the limiting factor, so it was the universal equalizer. Now the game depends on how many tokens you want to throw at the problem, and there are many bad actors with incentives to outspend every white hacker out there.Responsible disclosure will still be important, of course, but timelines will need to be compressed into days, instead of months.reply

There is case to be made that with the LLM-powered vulnerability research any bug found with the help of an LLM should be considered public.If I spent N tokens to find a specific funky bug, you should expect others to have done the same. title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients (newscientist.com)
comments: My father died from pancreatic cancer in 2016. He was 54. I don't think I'm ever going to get over it. Otherwise healthy guy starts not feeling great, goes to the doctor, gets misdiagnosed a few times. After a few months of that gets told that it's pancreatic cancer and he has 10-12 months. 15 months later he was gone. When I see news like this it gives me such hope for other people.reply

Sorry for your loss.Misdiagnosis is very common with pancreatic cancer, it seems. My mum was complaining about stomach pains and sickness for a long time before they finally tested her for pancreatic cancer; before that, they had all sorts of theories about what it was, including tropical sprue. By the time she knew it was cancer, she was stage 4 with months to live. Thankfully, chemo kept her alive just long enough to meet her grandson, and also for assisted dying laws that had just passed in Victoria, Australia.Hope that one day no one else has to go through what we did.reply

There's not a "test" in the sense of a blood draw for pancreatic cancer. Diagnosis is made by getting a piece of tissue (not easy) and having a pathologist review it.At a bare minimum, you will need to have a mass large enough to be seen on CT scan, and then an endoscopic biopsy (among GI scopes, the endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography or ERCP is one of the most difficult). And even that may not get enough tissue for a diagnosis.So, yeah, failure to diagnose it is common - largely because it's almost impossible to diagnose early. I'm a doctor. We feel sick when these things happen. It's horrible for our patients.reply

Same with gallbladder. A common way to find out you have it is to have tumors elsewhere that are not liver/breast/lung cells when biopsied, ie. it’s metastatic and you are doomed.‘Cancer of unknown origin’ is a grim diagnosis.reply
Is it possible to do consistent scans to find cancer early? Like MRIs 2x per year and CTs once every 18 months (for example)? I’m guessing for most people this is simply a matter of cost?reply

It has to be big enough to show up, and CT uses X rays, which are themselves carcinogenic (ionizing radiation).You will find abnormalities on both. They are likely to be nothing, but having found them, they must be investigated. The investigations are not risk-free because they are necessarily invasive. Bad things happen stochastically: there is always a chance.reply

> but having found them, they must be investigatedYou don't. This is the same reasoning why not to check for breast cancer.You can take multiple measurements and only act when something appears to be getting worse.reply
dont be too south korea pilled. you can never know second and third order effects from persistent scanning.reply

Yes and No. If insurance/money isn't an issue, then it helps to get a scan to detect cancers earlier but expose yourself to radiation which theoretically leads to more cancer. Few scans here and there, that risk is low. Issue is when you are dealing with just a few tumor cells, it's too small to see yet on traditional imaging. You might get the scan in March and already have a cancer just too small to detect then by Sept you have your 2nd scan and bam there it is and it's had enough time to seed your body. There is a whole set of medicine dedicated to those with money to do surveillance imaging (whole body MRIs) hoping to catch things early, but the data isn't there. Even the ACR (American College of Radiology) recommends against it (for now). ACR can change its guidelines in the future. We have had the same with prostate cancer and PSAs. For decades, USPSTF and other bodies recommended against annual PSAs due to false positives, but after decades of data, now the American Cancer Society recommends for PSAs since it has shown to be of benefit nowadays.I think our future will be tumor markers for early cancer detection. But in the meantime, do your screenings, do risk modification (ie don't smoke or excessively drink). Get to know your family history and if something isn't right with your body, seek medical help and find someone who is willing to listen.I know it's probably not what you want to hear, but our bodies have a shelf life. The longer we are alive, the higher our cancer risks. Do what your can to screen, but sometimes your genes predispose you to cancers and that's not something we can modify ... atleast right now. Hopefully soon we have a huge breakthrough in true tumor markers that are more accurate and maybe these new mRNA cancer vaccines are the breakthrough we need much like when we got the first Hepatitis C treatments.--Not a Radiologist or Oncologist, just your local Family Medicine MD and HN Nerdreply

This is so important to point out. Lots of serious diseases don't have a simple blood test that somehow doctors won't do out of hubris. I don't think most people understand what its like to actually diagnose things like pancreatic cancer, and a lot of other cancers.The NIH says more than half of cancer deaths come from types of cancer that lack established screening tests. This is just scary stuff. At a certain point, blaming doctors and hospitals doesn't make sense. We just don't have the technology for easy detection of many cancers and by the time doctors figure it out, the disease has to be advanced enough to be detected by them. That advanced stage often means treatment is difficult or impossible.reply
